name: Co-washing

lead: Co-washing means cleansing hair with conditioner rather than shampoo. People with dry, curly, textured, sensitive or chemically treated hair use it to keep moisture in and cut frizz, so curls look smoother and more defined.

Cleansing conditioners use milder cleansing agents and conditioning ingredients, so they remove less oil and product than shampoo while coating the strand. A 2019 dermatology review describes it as gentle but prone to buildup under the cuticle.

paras: Conditioner is worked into the scalp and hair in place of shampoo and rinsed out. It cleans less thoroughly, so it is often alternated with a clarifying shampoo, and silicone-free formulas are generally described as preferred.
The main reported issue is residue buildup under the cuticle. No safety concerns beyond ordinary cosmetic irritation are documented in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Users with dry, curly or textured hair co-wash to keep moisture in and cut frizz, so curls look smoother and more defined. The mild cleansing leaves more oil on the hair. A 2019 review describes it as gentle but prone to buildup.

lead: Co-washing, short for conditioner washing, is the practice of cleansing hair with a conditioner or a dedicated cleansing conditioner instead of shampoo.[1][2] People use it to keep hair softer, less frizzy and more defined, which is why it is associated with dry, sensitive, chemically processed or textured and curly hair, where over-cleansing can leave strands rough.[1][2]

A 2019 dermatology review describes overcleansed frizzy hair as cosmetically unacceptable and presents co-washing, with a conditioner free of silicones, petrolatum and mineral oils, as a gentle alternative that has become popular among people with sensitive hair. It also reports that residue can build up under the cuticle scales.[1] Wikipedia notes that cleansing conditioners clean less thoroughly than shampoo and are often alternated with a clarifying shampoo.[2]
Co-washing sits within the broader 'no-poo' movement, which rejects frequent shampooing; Wikipedia notes that some adherents rinse hair only with conditioner.[3]
infobox: Conditioner or cleansing conditioner in place of shampoo[2]
Dry, sensitive, chemically treated, curly hair[2]

paras: Conventional shampoo uses surfactants to remove oil and dirt, and it can leave hair rougher and more negatively charged, which is why conditioner is usually applied afterward.[2] Co-washing skips the shampoo step. Conditioners contain cationic surfactants, fatty alcohols and other agents that mainly coat the strand, and cleansing conditioners add milder cleansing agents.[2]
Practitioners are described as avoiding insoluble silicones in co-wash products to limit buildup.[2]

A review in Skin Appendage Disorders, titled as weighing the pros and cons of cleansing conditioners, frames shampoo over-cleansing as a cosmetic problem for frizzy hair and presents co-washing as a method that has become popular among people with sensitive hair. It reports gentleness to hair alongside a risk of residue buildup.[1]
Wikipedia reports that cleansing conditioners are generally recommended for dry, sensitive, chemically processed or textured hair and are often alternated with a clarifying shampoo.[2]

The no-poo movement rejects frequent shampooing; adherents use alternatives such as baking soda, vinegar, diluted honey, eggs or flours, and some rinse with conditioner only. Wikipedia says baking soda has been linked to hair damage and skin irritation, and that sulfate-free shampoos use alternative surfactants whose efficacy is still debated.[3]

Co-washing is discussed in hair-care circles as part of routines for curly and textured hair. Looksmaxxing forums that cover hair mostly discuss styling, hairlines and loss treatments, and the sources reviewed contain little material specific to co-washing there.
No studies found. A 2019 narrative review discusses the advantages and drawbacks of cleansing conditioners but is not a trial of appearance outcomes.[1]
